summary:
Space mission design is a balancing act. A small change to the payload or orbit can set off a chain reaction across power, thermal limits, mass and crew safety.. Traditional learning tools often treat these topics as separate dry entries in spreadsheets. That’s where Orbital Pulse comes in.

Orbital Pulse is a story-driven multiplayer simulation game. It supports 1, 2 or 4 players. The game is modeled after NASA’s Mission Design Lab and JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–5). Built with Python it includes real-time 3D trajectory visuals. Players take on roles in a Mission Control deck. They move through five campaigns. The missions start with configuring an Earth-observing CubeSat. They end with stabilizing an injured astronaut during a solar storm.

The game combines conversation-driven crises. It includes an on-demand "Urspace Guide" -tutorial system. It also features an "Astro-Calculus" hint-refill terminal. These tools help players understand the connections, between systems. Of memorizing isolated facts players experience how a space mission works as a single integrated system.

By making the learning process collaborative and time Orbital Pulse turns abstract systems engineering into an intuitive experience. Students and aspiring innovators don’t just learn about space missions. They. Feel how every decision affects the whole mission.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Orbital Pulse is an interactive, story-driven space mission design game inspired by NASA’s Mission Design Lab (MDL) and JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–5). Instead of using boring, complicated spreadsheets, our game puts 1, 2, or 4 players inside a futuristic Mission Control interface. Here, every single change you make directly impacts your spacecraft's mass, power, temperature, communication links, and crew safety in real time.

Players work their way through five story levels, starting easy and getting harder:

  • Level 1: Building a 6U CubeSat in Low Earth Orbit for landslide mapping and stem-cell testing.
  • Level 2: Designing a deep-space telescope at Lagrange Point 2 (L2) cooled down to -230°C.
  • Level 3: Drilling for water-ice inside the permanently dark Shackleton Crater on the Moon.
  • Level 4: Handling a mid-mission medical emergency where an astronaut is injured during a spacewalk right before a solar storm hits.
  • Level 5: A 14-month crewed mission to anchor onto and mine a metallic asteroid 2.2 AU away.

In the background, our physics engine automatically calculates launch mass limits, solar power drops over distance (1/r²), battery drain during eclipses, and data transmission limits.

How Our Project is Creative

  • Flexible Multiplayer Modes: Whether you play solo (with AI teammates), as a duo, or in a 4-player squad using a live room code, the game smoothly connects five major areas: Electrical Power, Avionics/Comms, Mechanical/Thermal systems, Resource Extraction (ISRU), and Space Biomedicine.
  • Live Crisis Decisions: Instead of just building a spacecraft and watching it fly, sudden emergencies pause the mission. For example, if an astronaut has internal bleeding in Level 4, the team has to vote under pressure: stabilize them in zero-gravity using telemedicine, or burn extra fuel (Delta-v) for a fast 72-hour return to Earth that risks a dangerous 5.5G re-entry.
  • Built-in Learning & Puzzle Refills: We added an on-demand "Urspace Guide" that pauses the game timer for 45 seconds to show quick 20-second visual tutorials whenever a player gets stuck on a hard concept. Players also get 5 diagnostic hints, and if they run out, they can solve real math and space physics problems in the "Astro-Calculus Terminal" to refill their hints and earn bonus points.

Factors We Considered & Intended Impact We wanted the game to be fair for everyone, regardless of team size or experience. That is why we created a Fair-Play Time System that gives solo players extra time to manage all four stations, splits speed bonuses 50/50 between individual and team performance in multiplayer, and never punishes beginners for opening tutorials. Our main goal is to help students move beyond memorized textbook formulas and actually experience how real NASA engineers collaborate, solve problems, and balance trade-offs as a team.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Backend & Physics: Python (OOP), NumPy, and SciPy to run the orbital math, power calculations, link budgets, and GMAT-based equations.
  • Frontend & 3D Graphics: NiceGUI and Streamlit with custom dark-mode glassmorphic CSS, SVG gauges, and Plotly 3D for the interactive 3D orbit globe and live 6-axis trade-off radar chart.
  • Multiplayer System: FastAPI and WebSockets for real-time team syncing, 4-digit room codes, and live crisis voting.
